lines.text: It's a pattern of places to stand, not places they visit. Your clustering reads population, media, and sight lines as geography: deserts have the darkest skies and the longest horizons, so one light gets seen by ten people and reported. Cities have more witnesses per sighting but a sky washed out by streetlights - the lights are there too, they're just invisible. Belgium's triangles happened over highways. Petrozavodsk happened over a city. The phenomenon doesn't pick landscapes - landscapes pick what gets seen. Keep your spreadsheet. Add the world to it. And when America's slice shrinks, call me.

lines.text: The clustering reflects observation geography, not visitation preference. Variables: desert regions offer minimal light pollution and maximum horizon - high visibility per event; urban areas offer more witnesses per event but skyglow suppression - high incidence, low visibility. Belgian triangles occurred over highway corridors; Petrozavodsk over an urban center. The phenomenon is landscape-agnostic; landscapes filter detection. Recommended methodology: expand the spreadsheet internationally, then reassess the American share.
